mcqs: National income, employment and inflation are studied in macro economics.
Pakistan uses all three methods — production, expenditure and factor incomes — to measure national income.
Pakistan is basically an agricultural country.
Among the given sectors, agriculture has the largest share in Pakistan's real GDP.
The sports goods industry (Sialkot) is largely a cottage/small-scale industry.
Meier and Baldwin gave a comprehensive definition: economic development is a process whereby an economy's real national income increases over a long period of time.
Language does not affect economic development; resources, political conditions and social evils do.
Economic development means a sustained increase in real national (and per capita) income.

s: The Second Five-Year Plan (1960–65) is generally regarded as Pakistan's most successful plan; it exceeded its growth target.
mcqs.n: The book ticks (b) third plan here, but in Unit 9 Q13 it ticks the second plan as the successful one; the Second Plan is the accepted answer.

mcqs: The Second Five-Year Plan covered 1960 to 1965.
Developing countries lack capital; a heavy quantity of capital is not their characteristic.
Major industries were nationalised in 1972 (Z. A. Bhutto's government).
longQuestions: (1) Low per capita income; (2) Rapid population growth — large families with few earners; (3) Unemployment and disguised unemployment; (4) Inflation — rising prices reduce real income; (5) Unequal distribution of income and wealth.

(6) Low productivity of agriculture and industry; (7) Illiteracy and lack of technical skills; (8) Poor health facilities and nutrition; (9) Shortage of capital and low saving and investment; (10) Shortage of energy (electricity, gas).

(11) Political instability, corruption and bad governance; (12) Heavy burden of foreign debt; (13) Social evils — extravagance on ceremonies, dowry; (14) Under-utilisation of natural resources; (15) Inadequate infrastructure and housing.

(1) Rapid growth of population (about 2% a year) divides national income among more people; (2) Low productivity in agriculture due to old methods, small holdings and shortage of water; (3) Slow industrial growth; (4) Shortage of capital — low savings and investment.

(5) Illiteracy and lack of technical education reduce efficiency of labour; (6) Unemployment and disguised unemployment; (7) Under-utilisation of natural resources; (8) Energy shortages; (9) Unequal distribution of wealth — feudal system and concentration in few hands.

(10) Political instability and law-and-order problems discourage investment; (11) Heavy defence expenditure and debt servicing; (12) Inflation; (13) Corruption and inefficient administration; (14) Natural disasters such as floods and droughts.

The reasons are: high population growth rate; dependence on backward agriculture; small and slowly growing industrial base; shortage of capital and technology; low literacy and skills; unemployment; underdeveloped natural resources; shortage of electricity and gas.

Also: unequal distribution of income (landlords and industrialists hold most wealth); corruption and bad governance; political instability; heavy foreign debt and defence burden; inflation; low exports and trade deficit; social customs causing wasteful spending; and natural calamities.

(1) Control population growth through family planning and education; (2) Modernise agriculture — improved seeds, fertilisers, machinery, irrigation and credit; (3) Rapid industrialisation, especially agro-based and small industries; (4) Increase saving and investment; encourage foreign investment.

(5) Develop human resources — education, technical training and health; (6) Overcome energy shortages by building dams and using alternative energy; (7) Exploit natural resources (minerals, gas, coal); (8) Increase exports and reduce unnecessary imports.

(9) Political stability and good law and order; (10) Remove corruption and improve governance; (11) Fair distribution of wealth through land reforms and progressive taxation; (12) Economic planning; (13) Enforcement of the Islamic economic system (zakat, ushr, interest-free economy); (14) Develop infrastructure — roads, communications, IT.

Economic factors: (1) Natural resources — land, minerals, water, forests; (2) Capital formation — saving and investment; (3) Human resources — educated, skilled and healthy labour; (4) Technology and innovation; (5) Entrepreneurship; (6) Infrastructure — transport, communications, energy; (7) Size of the market and foreign trade.

Non-economic factors: (1) Political stability and good governance; (2) Law and order; (3) Social values — honesty, hard work, absence of social evils; (4) Education and attitudes towards change; (5) Sound institutions (banks, courts); (6) Population control; (7) Economic planning and sound government policies; (8) International cooperation, aid and peace.

(1) Shortage of energy — load-shedding of electricity and gas; (2) Shortage of capital and high interest rates; (3) Outdated machinery and lack of modern technology; (4) Shortage of skilled labour and managers; (5) Dependence on imported raw materials and machinery.

(6) Political instability and inconsistent industrial policies; (7) Law-and-order problems and labour disputes; (8) High taxes and complicated procedures; (9) Limited domestic market and competition from foreign (smuggled) goods; (10) Lack of research and development.
(11) Concentration on a few industries (textiles); (12) Sick units and poor management; (13) Inadequate infrastructure; (14) Corruption and red tape; (15) Under-utilisation of installed capacity.

Importance and benefits of economic planning: (1) Efficient use of limited resources according to national priorities; (2) Rapid economic growth and increase in national and per capita income; (3) Removal of unemployment; (4) Balanced development of all sectors and regions.

(5) Reduction in inequalities of income and wealth; (6) Development of infrastructure (dams, roads, power); (7) Industrialisation and modernisation of agriculture; (8) Price stability and control of inflation; (9) Mobilisation of savings and capital formation.

(10) Improvement of social services — education, health, housing; (11) Self-reliance — less dependence on foreign aid; (12) Improvement in balance of payments; (13) Coordination between public and private sectors; (14) Achievement of a welfare state.

(1) Increase national and per capita income through a high growth rate; (2) Provide employment opportunities and reduce poverty; (3) Increase agricultural production and achieve self-sufficiency in food; (4) Rapid industrialisation; (5) Develop human resources — literacy, technical education and health.

(6) Develop energy resources and infrastructure; (7) Reduce income inequality and regional imbalances; (8) Control population growth; (9) Increase exports and reduce the trade deficit; (10) Control inflation and keep prices stable; (11) Reduce dependence on foreign loans; (12) Improve housing, water supply and the environment; (13) Promote science and IT; (14) Establish an Islamic welfare state.
